content: Pine bark extract, derived from species of the Pinus genus, is rich in bioflavonoids, particularly proanthocyanidins, which are known for their antioxidant properties. These supplements are marketed for the prevention and treatment of various chronic conditions linked to oxidative stress. This review aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of pine bark extract in managing chronic disorders. The review included 27 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 1641 participants, assessing the effects of pine bark extract on 10 chronic conditions: asthma, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), cardiovascular disease (CVD) and associated risk factors, chronic venous insufficiency (CVI), diabetes mellitus (DM), erectile dysfunction, female sexual dysfunction, osteoarthritis, osteopenia, and traumatic brain injury. The trials varied in duration, ranging from four weeks to six months, and most used a placebo as the control. The overall risk of bias was low in four studies, high in one, and unclear in the remaining 22 studies. In adults with asthma, the evidence was of very low certainty, and it remains unclear whether pine bark extract improves lung function (measured by forced expiratory volume in one second [FEV1] and forced vital capacity [FVC]), alleviates asthma symptoms, or reduces the need for albuterol inhalers. In children with ADHD, the evidence was also of very low certainty. It is uncertain whether pine bark extract reduces inattention and hyperactivity (as assessed by parent and teacher rating scales) or improves visual-motor coordination and concentration. For participants with cardiovascular disease, the evidence was of very low certainty. It is unclear whether pine bark extract reduces diastolic blood pressure, increases HDL cholesterol, or decreases LDL cholesterol. In individuals with chronic venous insufficiency, the evidence was of very low certainty. It is uncertain whether pine bark extract reduces pain scores, increases the resolution of pain, or improves physician-assessed treatment efficacy. In type 2 diabetes mellitus, the evidence was of very low certainty. It is unclear whether pine bark extract reduces fasting blood glucose levels or decreases HbA1c. Similarly, in a mixed group of participants with type 1 and type 2 diabetes, it is uncertain whether pine bark extract reduces HbA1c levels. In men with erectile dysfunction, the evidence was of very low certainty, and it remains unclear whether pine bark extract improves erectile function as measured by the International Index of Erectile Function-5. In women with sexual dysfunction, the evidence was of very low certainty. It is uncertain whether pine bark extract improves satisfaction (as measured by the Female Sexual Function Index) or reduces pain scores. In adults with knee osteoarthritis, the evidence was of very low certainty. It is unclear whether pine bark extract reduces composite scores on the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index or decreases the use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. In postmenopausal women with osteopenia, the evidence was of very low certainty. It is uncertain whether pine bark extract increases bone alkaline phosphatase levels. In individuals with traumatic brain injury, the evidence was of very low certainty. It is unclear whether pine bark extract reduces cognitive failure scores or post-concussion symptoms. Across most conditions, the studies did not report on hospital admissions or serious adverse events. Due to small sample sizes, limited numbers of RCTs for each condition, variability in outcome measures, and poor reporting, no definitive conclusions can be drawn regarding the efficacy or safety of pine bark extract supplements for treating chronic disorders.
